do you realize that your car runs most efficiently when your foot is off the gas/coasting? And that restarting your engine after coasting downhill with the engine off almost certainly uses more gas that you hoped to save?
sure, if he coasts a whole mile out without power he might come out ahead
But I'm curious to know if you have any offhand numbers on how much gas a car uses while coasting, and how much it uses for the start process.

When your car is coasting, the injectors don't even need to put any fuel in the engine as the wheels are turning the engine.

I built a custom engine for my first car. I was older 12v inline 6 engine cobbled together by two dudes with off the shelf aftermarket parts, parts swapped from other car models, a hand-built ECU built from kit running open-source tuning software. On start-up with a cold the injectors were set to dump 5-50% extra fuel for the first 5 minutes (a cold-start cycle determined by engine temp; 50% extra at 0 degrees Celcius, 5% extra at 90 degrees Celcius, a linear progression in between). This is done in part because it's needed to keep the engine running and in part because it's easier/safer on the engine components until everythings heats up to normal operating temperatures.

With that engine we had the injectors set to 0% duty cycle at, IIRC, -100kPa intake manifold pressure detected AKA throttle body closed coasting foot off the pedal.

Every engine is different, so it's impossible to really have number to throw up; the information above was my experience. Also, that specific case varies from that of @whateverhisnameis up there who turns off his camry to coast down hills, his car isn't gonna cool to the point where it would need a cold-start cycle to get running, assuming it was at full operating temp before getting to the top of the hill.

I'm also williing to admit that contemporary engines with much more advanced computers, r&d, and money put into engineering them are definitely more efficient in the start/warm up process but it's still asinine to bother turning off the car to coast down a hill to save gas with an immeasurably worthless ROI.

Basically, he was some weird old fellow who would travel through the usual pubs of the city and sit down at the tables of random people without any kind of invitation, offering - or rather, insisting - to make a pencil drawing of everyone at said tables in exchange for a very modest sum of Euros.

While this understandably could be rather annoying if one did not want to be drawn, the sheer fact that he had followed this tradition since the 90s and 364 days a year strongly endeared him to the pub-going people of Bonn, and although nobody knew his actual name or who he was, his recent death lead to anything from galleries with his art being hosted in the pubs he used to frequent to petitions to name a street after him.
